title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) comparing an LLM‑only generation pipeline to a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator. All planned pairs completed (complete_pairs = 200), consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, deterministic execution accounting, the randomized 10% Mininet holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models promises productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but creates operational risk when generated changes are semantically incorrect or unsafe. A common mitigation architecture is generate–validate–repair (GVR), where a deterministic validator checks generated candidates and an LLM is asked to repair failing outputs. Prior work proposes validator‑assisted pipelines and documents LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and configuration brittleness. However, the practical marginal benefit of automated repair depends on baseline validator‑detectable failure prevalence, validator fidelity, and the repair budget. We therefore preregistered a narrowly scoped, externally auditable confirmatory question: for a fixed generator output per task, does invoking deterministic validation and at most one automated repair materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to applying the raw LLM candidate?
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies across LLM applications report hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation strategies include retrieval grounding, verifier assistance, and constrained agent architectures. NetOps prototypes establish feasibility of intent→configuration generation but often lack instrumented, preregistered evaluations that quantify operational failure rates. Architectural proposals and prototype systems recommend pairing LLMs with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checks) and guarded agent patterns; independent red‑team audits highlight configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes. Our study complements this literature by providing a preregistered, paired measurement that isolates the marginal effect of validator+repair on identical generator outputs under a constrained, reproducible adapter policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) defined a paired binary design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and at most one automated repair call if the primary validator reported violations. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the confirmatory test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were computed with a bootstrap percentile procedure (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Planned maximum model calls = 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs); the adapter enforced per‑task and global caps and deterministic shared‑initial semantics.

Task bank and validators. We used a machine‑checkable intent→configuration task bank of 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial/final states, workflow constraints, and a required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect primary‑validator blind spots.

Sampling determinism and adapter enforcement. The model configuration recorded the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and lists a null temperature field in the archived model configuration. Deterministic behaviour was achieved by the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter which enforced a single shared initial generation per task and reused that candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions. Deterministic_reconciliation artifacts from execution accounting confirm hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, substantiating the enforced shared‑initial semantics. The shared‑initial paired design intentionally removes sampling variance across conditions to isolate the marginal effect of invoking validation and a single repair prompt on the identical generator output; this is a preplanned trade‑off and is documented in the preregistration.

Repair policy, handling, and contamination plan. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM when the primary validator reported violations. Repaired candidates would be re‑validated and recorded. The contamination plan used the Mininet emulator on a randomized 10% holdout to flag any validator–emulator disagreement; flagged pairs would be excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered conservative rule. Note on reproducibility: the contamination summary reports zero disagreements in the 20‑task holdout, but the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw that holdout is not present among the labeled artifacts, which limits exact bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the holdout draw and is therefore disclosed explicitly (see Reproducibility statement below).
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes without technical failures (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z). Model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair calls used = 0; maximum_model_calls = 400. Adapter/provider audit artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, confirming single shared invocations per task as preregistered.

Primary outcomes and exact inference. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction could not be evaluated on this dataset.

Secondary outcomes and contamination check. No validator failures occurred; consequently the repair branch was never exercised and the exploratory secondary estimands (average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical data in this run. The preregistered Mininet 10% holdout produced zero validator–emulator disagreement flags in the contamination summary, consistent with the validator verdicts on that sample. As noted above, the holdout draw’s explicit selection seed is not present among labeled artifacts, limiting exact reproducibility of the specific holdout despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The artifact‑grounded null outcome is precise: under the chosen generator/prompt policy and the shared‑initial deterministic design, there were no validator‑detectable failures for GVR to reduce. This does not prove that GVR is generally ineffective; rather, it shows that the marginal utility of automated repair depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage for a given production policy. The shared‑initial design isolates the causal contrast between applying an unchecked candidate and validating (and possibly repairing) that exact candidate; it intentionally excludes benefits obtainable through resampling or stochastic ensembles.

Why initial candidates passed. Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count matched required_command_count and that validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true for sampled tasks. Difficulty labels in the task bank ("medium", "hard", "very_hard") and patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change indicate the benchmark exercised nontrivial dependency constraints even when outputs were correct. These artifacts explain why the primary validator observed zero failures.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and deterministic reconciliation confirming accounting. Construct validity is limited by the validator’s expressiveness: deterministic validators codify a finite set of checks and may miss device idiosyncrasies. External validity is constrained by a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), shared‑initial deterministic sampling, the curated task bank, and the single repair budget (≤1 repair call per task). Conclusion validity: with zero discordant observations the confirmatory McNemar test is uninformative about the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction, but the null result is an exact, artifact‑verifiable outcome for the preregistered estimand.

Operational implications and guidance. Practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence under the intended generation policy and validate validator completeness with richer emulation or device tests before deciding repair budgets. Where baseline failures are rare, resources may be better allocated to expanding validator fidelity, adversarial testing, multi‑sample generation, or human‑in‑the‑loop processes. When baseline failures are nontrivial, GVR with an appropriate repair budget and richer repair strategies can reduce validator‑detectable errors; the preregistered plan here documents how to instrument and account for those interventions.

Reproducibility statement (explicit gap). All execution artifacts required to audit the run are archived in the execution bundle (model calls, task manifests, validator traces, analysis tables, deterministic reconciliation). The randomized 10% Mininet holdout produced zero disagreements per the contamination summary, but the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw that holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this omission prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of which tasks comprised that holdout and we prominently disclose this limitation here.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired study (n = 200) comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial semantics. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent on this curated workload, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. The artifact‑grounded outcome emphasizes that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent and recommends that future confirmatory evaluations target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, increase repair budgets and sampling diversity, scale secondary emulation checks (while recording selection seeds), and evaluate model and deployment diversity to better characterize operational gains.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent and constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the contamination summary shows zero disagreements for that holdout but the explicit randomized selection seed for that holdout is not present among the labeled artifacts (reproducibility gap disclosed above). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z); model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
